utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to all. May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Crispian Smith for the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, Dragan Krgovic for Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is one preliminary matter which I would like to raise with your leave, at this moment before the witness enters court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, it came to my attention yesterday when I was reading the transcript that a part of yesterday's session was a closed session when we were discussing 92 ter application. I analysed it, there's nothing confidential in it, and I would like to move the Trial Chamber to leave the confidentiality of this part of the transcript. Thank you very much. Yes, it was in a closed -- private session, I'm sorry, private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was the question of whether or not I had complied with the formula on 92 ter. And one of Your Honours, I can't remember which, said we ought to go into private session. So that's what the discussion was about. I don't have any strong feelings one way or the other about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, the ruling is that -- yes, the ruling is revisited and those proceedings which you recall as being in private session are now open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, may we have the witness back on the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I remind you you are still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, we are now going to have a look at one of the documents that related to the ministerial counsel which we looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's 65 ter 1472, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's dated the 13th of January, the minutes, but it actually relates to the -- a meeting on the 11th of January of 1992. And we can see listed there the people who attended. Minutes, do you know who took the minutes of these meetings? If we go to the end, and I don't want to go to the end for the moment, but there's somebody called the ministerial council secretary, Drasko Vuleta. Would he have taken the minutes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. That was far away from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, what was far away from you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minutes - about who was leading the ministerial council at the time, I don't remember. I wasn't there, I mean, that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you were at this meeting. If we look at the attendees, we can see that you are listed as the first, second, third, fourth, fifth person; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not contesting that. You are asking me about who took the minutes, and I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine. Don't worry. We can see also that Mico Stanisic attended and also Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik. Rajko Dukic, president of the executive committee of the SDS; and Mr. Cancar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Could we go, please, in the English to the second page, and in the B/C/S also to the second page. And I want the second paragraph under item 2, please, up, thank you, and the last paragraph in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As you told us yesterday, there had been the declaration in January of the republic of the Serbian people, and there was then a discussion. And one can see it said there: "It was concluded that the priorities springing from the declaration included the defining of ethnic territory, the establishment of government organs in the territory, and the economic disempowerment of the current authorities in the socialist republic of BH." Now, what was meant by the defining of ethnic territory? It may be obvious, Mr. Djeric, but perhaps you can explain to the Court.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest that was within the purview of the party and with the purview of the assembly of the Serbian people when it comes to those political goals. I really can't talk about that in any detail. I can't provide any explanation. That was within the purview of that party and within the purview of the leadership of the Serbian people at the time. The only thing that I might say is that it was about the regionalisation or deregionalisation that was at the forefront at the time. And those were the ideas that were the focus of all the thoughts and considerations, if I have been of any help with that. So nothing went beyond those ideas and that framework. Those ideas and that platform was the basis of all the discussions, it was a time of transition, the former communist system was being replaced by a new democratic system, you will remember of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, but you were present at this meeting, when it said that the -- when whoever raised it said that ethnic territory had to be defined, did they explain what was meant by that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember, but there were discussions about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Establishment of government organs in the territory, what was meant by that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always in this period of regions and regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] All right. Yes, but whose government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the government of the region, the government of the region. But it wasn't in dispute that when it came to defining the regions the ethnic criteria will play the prevalent role, that was not in dispute. There were a criteria of course that were the basis of all that, but the prevalent criterion was the ethnic criterion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All I'm asking is what was the ethnic criteria? Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time it was the peoples that every people in Bosnia and Herzegovina should have its territory, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predominantly. Which means that there was a certain set of criteria, the fact that people were historically living there. This is not something that I was ever dealing with. I'm just trying to help you and I'm trying to remember what was discussed at the time, and that what was discussed is exactly what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you've said that the criteria was that the fact that people were historically living there. So not who was living there at the present in the territory, but who had historically lived there, was that the criteria?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I mean, this is not something I would have dealt with. I'm just helping -- I'm just telling you that this was discussed. There were all sorts of discussions going on. There were discussions about the ethnicity, history, this and that and the other, but all that is far from me. The criteria, history, ethnicity, all that is beyond me, and there's nothing special I can add to that or I can't remember. It's all foggy. It's all as if through the mist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You've said that it was to -- the criteria for everyone. Are you saying that the defining of ethnic territory was for Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, that's what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean discussions were going on about that and I, as the minister of development at that time on the eve of the conflict I was also preoccupied with that amongst other things. There were discussions about that by the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina on the eve of the war, and we had all sorts of disputes going on because there were different visions and views.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. All I'm asking you, don't worry about what anybody was doing, at this meeting, was the discussion about the defining of ethnic territory, ethnic territory for all three nationalities or just one?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we are dealing with the Serbian regional territory or space, but I'm talking from the position of predominant ethnical criteria, but others were not excluded either. Awhile ago I told you that that issue was discussed even before the conflict and everything was said there, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina discussed that. There are recordings of those discussions, all of them should exist. So this is not -- I apologise --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, stop, please. Please stop. I'm not - and I've told you for the second time - interested in what was discussed at any other meetings other than this one. Now, can we one more time, the defining of ethnic territory, you said the criteria was historical. Does that mean it wasn't concerned with who was actually living in the territories that you were trying to define ethnically at the present time, in other words January of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I mean, this did not exclude other peoples. We are talking about regions, about formulating regions. But based on the ethnic criterion, the ethnic criterion was proclaimed to be predominant, primary, but other criteria and rights of the other people residing in those territories were not excluded as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to look at one other part of the minutes for this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, page 3 in the English, and also page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 of the conclusions: "A Working Group comprising Mico Stanisic, Dr. Zepinic..." somebody called Laic, I think it is, "... and Novakovic will deal with the issues regarding the organisation and scope of national security and will frame a concept about this. Mico Stanisic is responsible for the work of the group." Please, Mr. Djeric, we've got a number of documents to get through. What was Mico Stanisic going to be looking at? What does the scope of national security and framing a concept? What was he going to do?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's simply a question which I can't answer. I can't talk about that in any great detail. This was a matter for the assembly of the Serbian people and party leadership. I already said something about that yesterday. As to what that body was to be dealing with, what the matter of security was, I really can't -- simply I can't, I never dealt with that, I wasn't interested at the time, and therefore I can't say anything about that today, as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I'm not interest in whether it was your idea or at the moment whether you agreed with any of it. All I'm asking you is what was discussed. What was Mico Stanisic supposed to be doing in respect of security?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He got from the -- we are talking about the ministerial council here, are we not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He received his tasks from the president of the ministerial council. I suppose there must be documents to that effect. I wasn't -- I can't remember that discussion and the details about that. I don't remember the discussion at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In the -- what the Court has heard, at the end of March, beginning of April, the MUP split and a Serbian MUP was set up. Did this discussion have anything to do with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't establish a link between the two, I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's your final answer, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your final answer is you can't tell us anything about what Mico Stanisic was supposed to be doing, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that discussion. And as for any of the documents, they were never presented to me. I was never given those documents. It was a matter for the president of the ministerial council and the security organ, and so on and so forth. I can't say anything about that. I think that there wasn't a direct link between that and the events from the very beginning. Is there something wrong with my microphone?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so. Right. It has nothing to do with the eventual split in the MUP. Just think for a moment, would you, Mr. Djeric, what was it that Mico Stanisic was being tasked by the president or the SDS or Dr. Karadzic or whoever, what was he being tasked to do? Much as I hate that word.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I really don't know what tasks he received, but I told you yesterday it was the time of the peace accord which was discussed at the time. I'm talking about the Cutileiro plan, and I suppose that it was all about that. But I can't be sure of that. Well, you know, all the sides were studying that accord and trying to find their place in that accord and that plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about generalisations about the Cutileiro plan and what other sides were doing. I'm asking you specific questions about specific documents, and that's what I want you to answer, please. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's look an another document, a meeting of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I really -- I am trying to be very concrete, as concrete as I can be, to the best of my abilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's my intention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric. Can we look please at a meeting of the National Security Council. 65 ter 1164, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, while we are waiting for this next document, I just want to remind you that, of course, you are not in any way sought to be held responsible for any of the events that we are discussing here. The only thing we are trying to do is to get as objectively as we can some insight into the matters that were discussed at the time. And now that I have the floor, I just want to get back to one thing that you started out by saying in your testimony this morning; namely, that this was about regionalisation. And I'm not sure I fully understand what that means. Can you briefly explain to me the intention behind this and the rationality behind this concept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll try and briefly explain things for you. Before the conflict, as you know, we lived in one state which was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. What happened next were the events that you are already familiar with. You know that Yugoslavia is a multiethnic community, underwent certain things, as you know, and then in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were three peoples, including the Serbian people. And what happened was there was an existential fear because people felt that they were losing their general public good, which was their state. And of course people were concerned, and they were trying to find their place in the plans, and agreements that we are talking about. They were seeking to try -- seeking to protect their rights. And in that sense they wanted regions to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When you say that they were afraid of losing their state, can you explain this to me? Who was afraid of losing their state and who would come and take their state away from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I'm talking about the Serbian people. That's who I'm talking about. Because Yugoslavia was the ideal solution for that people. Because the Serb people lived everywhere in most of Yugoslavia, and they lived under a single umbrella in one state, and when Yugoslavia disappeared, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a place where an issue was raised. If a multiethnic community, such was Yugoslavia, could not exist and could not survive. The issue was whether Bosnia and Herzegovina could offer adequate solutions for all the peoples including the Serbs who lived there. I'm talking and I'm saying that the cessation resulted in problems and in a national homogenisation because there was existential fear present among people. My opinion is that it is bad practice to break up a multiethnic state, and this was proven. And I'm talking about the future. Let bygones be bygones, there's nothing we can do about that. That's my opinion. And then issues were raised within the framework of European regionalisation processes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at the meeting of the National Security Council. Looks like the minutes were produced on the the 18th of April, but the meeting was on the 16th. Could we look please at the second page in English, and it's also the second page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see that the minutes were signed by Radovan Karadzic as president of the council. Item number 10, it was decided to inform the SAOs about the display of symbols at the borders of Serbian Bosnian territory and then it goes on to the symbols, as well in -- each territory is proclaimed as Serbian territories, as one of those in which the authority of Serbian BH was later established formally occupied by the Green Berets. First of all, by the Green Berets, who is being referred to there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were certain armed units that were being meant, among the Bosniak people, maybe it was the SDA or the patriotic league. I don't know where they were from, but in any case these were armed formations within the Bosniak people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They didn't just mean Muslims generally?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It didn't just mean those of Muslim nationality; it meant literally armed men, did it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were in the function of the SDA, and the SDA policies. I don't know. I'm not going to go into the composition, but they were predominantly for sure. In any case, they were working on the implementation of the policy of the SDA as the leading party of the Bosniak Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you see, what it says here is, not only should the symbols be set up in what was proclaimed to be Serbian territory, but also in territories where the authority of the Serbs was to be established. Sir, is what was being discussed here, actual -- the forceful taking over of areas?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in what way? But the fact is that there was operating here with these territories which were -- which belonged to the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but who decided they belonged to the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the political leadership that charged certain cartographers who drew up those maps. I mean, I keep going back to these agreements. There were always some sort of maps in circulation, and then there were agreement that had to do with these maps. The maps didn't appear. They were circulating, they were already present at the negotiations, the peace talks, and they were already perhaps some agreements regarding some territories.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but we are way beyond the the peace talks now, aren't we? We are April 16th, war has -- or conflict has already started, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that, you know, negotiations were still going on. The plan, as far as I can remember was still in play.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But I'm looking simply at what is recorded and what is being talked about at this meeting that you were present at. That what is being said there, isn't it, is that the Serbs were going to take over territory that was not accepted as being Serbian? Bosnian Serb, I should say. Isn't that what was being said there, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please additionally repeat this question for me, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The sentence that Serbian -- "symbols are to be set up in territories in which the authority of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina was later established (formerly occupied by the Green Berets)." It really is a simple question, is what is being discussed there, the taking over of these territories by force?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the Green Berets were in these territories, then it's just a question of a counter-action here. Evidently, what we are talking about here are some disputed areas, disputed areas from these talks. The whole problem lay with the disputed territories. Only in Dayton were there boundaries established between Republika Srpska and the Bosnian Federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By April the 16th, Mr. Djeric, was it clear to you and everybody else that the Muslims were not accepting the declaration of what the Bosnian Serbs said was their territory? The answer is yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim side rejected that in the same way that the Serbian side rejected the forceful referendum on March 1st. The Muslim side declared -- denied the declaration, and the Serbian side denied the validity of the referendum. And things proceeded the way they proceeded. At the same time, the peace agreement was unfolding. Let me just remind you, Mr. Izetbegovic first accepted the agreement, he accepted the agreement, you have to count on that, and then subsequently rejected it. So it was in play, the agreement had been reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move to the next, because otherwise again we are going to get stuck on this document. Paragraph 11. "The attention of the MUP is drawn -- or was drawn to the infiltration of a large number of emigrants in JNA uniforms and wearing Serbian insignia, whose goal is the destruction of the legally elected Serbian authorities and the execution of various forms of sabotage..." Who were these emigrants whose goal was the destruction of the legally elected Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I think these are things that are connected to these structures, the police, the military, and they operated with that. So now I assume that these were these aggressive offensive party elements of the SDA, and so on and so forth. I think that's what this is about. But for me to be able to tell you any more, I simply never was in contact with any of that. Meaning, who was specifically there. These are some party militias and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, but as far as this council was concerned, it was the job of the MUP to deal with them, rather than the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about April?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. On the one hand, the MUP, but the army was present there too, you know. I think. This army was there, talks were being conducted about whether the army should stay there. So this should also be kept in mind, throughout April, talks were conducted for the JNA to remain in that area because of possible conflicts or, you know, security of factories, military facilities and so on, so this went on throughout the whole of April, these talks. But it was present, and for as long as it was present, I guess by definition its job was to deal with some form of security.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally, paragraph 16, please: "It was decided that a Commission to Determine War Crimes be formed." War crimes against whom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember at that time, but there was talk about crimes of all types, all types of crimes in relation to the Serbian people, and we will continue to persecute all the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it was war crimes against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours, the transcript did not reflect what precisely the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, Mr. Zecevic raised that you said something different. Your answer when I asked war crimes against whom, as recorded was: "I don't remember at that time, but there was talk about crimes of all types, all types of crimes in relation to the Serbian people, and we will continue to persecute all the crimes." Is that what you said, or did you say something different?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that these were all crimes no matter who committed them, and there was talk about crimes in relation to the Serbian people, but all other crimes too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So are you saying this was a commission that was to be set up to investigate war crimes whether committed by Serbs or against Serbs or Muslims or Croats; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the talk was in the sense that there was a commission that would deal with everything, but primarily and on a priority basis with the crimes on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I want to ask you about that group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Djeric, what do you mean with "the crimes on the Serbian side"? Do you mean crimes against Serbians or crimes committed by Serbians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the commission that was being discussed that would investigate all crimes, crimes against Serbian people and also by the Serbian side committed against others, but additionally what it had in mind were crimes against the Serbian people. This is not a question of ignoring the crimes that were committed by the Serbian side. These were not ignored. They were also -- the idea was also to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move to a different group of documents, and that's records of conversations that you had during the period April and May. I think we ought to put into context that on the 6th of April with the recognition of the independence of Bosnia by the EU, the police school at Vraca was taken over, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you've had an opportunity, I think, to listen to records of four different -- sorry, five different conversations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just to identify them, the first was a conversation between you and Mico Stanisic which has a date -- there were two different copies of it, but I think you say that the first is recorded as happening on the 18th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up on the screen -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object as you are put on notice by our motion on oral -- all intercepts. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we semi discussed this, and I thought that where -- that the witness can identify his own voice and that of the person to whom he is speaking, then the objection was withdrawn, other than the general objection that the intercepts were illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a couple of levels of our -- in our motion. The legality of the intercepts, the preconditions for that, plus the authenticity. And in case where the witness is the one who is on the tape and can remember his -- the occasion and the person who he is talking to, obviously then he can authenticate this conversation. But the objection still stands. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm in your hands, I mean, this all came in very late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My recollection is, and this is probably two days ago, that in terms of the different categories which counsel have identified, that the jurisprudence on the question of these intercepts being so well settled, your objection is noted for the record. But there is, as Ms. Korner has indicated, as I recall, and counsel will correct me if I'm wrong, no live issue in terms of where, as with what she now proposes to put, the witness is able to identify his own voice, isn't that where we are?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly where we are, Your Honour, but our motion -- our motion has different -- different aspects of objection to the admission of intercepts as an exhibit. This one concerning the authenticity in the particular case can be probably remedied in case the witness can confirm that this is the contents of the -- that these are the precise contents of his speech with this other person and identify the other person. I understand that. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I deal with it this way then, I won't go into the actual content, I mean, it speaks for itself in any event for most of them, and simply get the witness until we ruled on this motion, which, I may say, I do find strange because these intercepts have been in other cases on a number of occasions, but -- and simply I'd get him to identify the intercepts, and then we'll see where we go. I mean, the content does speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may just add one thing, I know of course we are fully aware that there is a jurisprudence on the intercepts before this Tribunal. However, this is the first, I think, case where our position is backed up by the forensic findings, forensic institute, where they say clearly that the authenticity cannot be confirmed. That is the first case before this Tribunal as far as I can -- as far as I know and we researched that, that the authenticity was backed up -- the authenticity issue was backed up with the findings of the forensic institute which is a clearly an expert body which did a lot of expertise for the Prosecution before this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So now you are saying, Mr. Zecevic, that the authenticity issue is the most important one. The other one, you know, you are referring to the jurisprudence of the -- which you seem to accept. Well, "accept" is perhaps a little bit too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's a little bit more complex than that. I think it has to be regarded and addressed in its totality. The authenticity, the legality, and everything. All the aspects of the intercept, that's our position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we made the point. You know, they've got this so-called expert report in July. They file a motion about this when a witness is about to appear who is going to deal with evidence. I am afraid Mr. Zecevic can't have it both ways. I'm suggesting, however, that the way of dealing with it so far is an aspect that you will want to consider is whether a witness is able to identify his voice and that of the person to whom he is speaking. As I say, at this stage, I'm only asking the witness to do that, and I cannot see that that is not admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the forensic report was done on July, and it was done based on the intercepts which have been disclosed to us in the pretrial phase. By filing the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution changed the mandate, the intercepts and added quite a few new ones. And we were exploring the possibility of having additional resources to address these additionally disclosed intercepts with the forensic institute; however, we failed with that because -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we have read the report also, of course. And while it is true that the report does conclude that it cannot be established with any degree of full certainty that these tapes are authentic, the report actually also does say that there are no traces of these tapes having been tampered with. So I think that if the witness can confirm that it is his voice and can confirm that the other partner with whom he was speaking was your client, then I think at least for this tape, for this recording we would go ahead and should go ahead and confront it now to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. But that is exactly what I was talking about, but we still object to the intercepts as such being admitted as evidence, for the reasons we stated in our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We are taking note of that. Ms. Korner, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we just go through the intercepts. We'll have them quickly, the transcript on the screen. The first is a conversation between you and Mico Stanisic. It's number is 2877.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's actually, as you pointed out, I think, the first version seem to have a date of May, but the date is the 18th of April, and you are speaking to him at Vraca school; is that right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please -- around the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you've got some documents there, Mr. Djeric, can you tell us what you are looking for? I see you've got the transcripts there.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are transcripts, but the date here is a little bit -- I'm not sure about the date. Can you -- can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, stop for a moment. I'm not interested in the date, I'm not interested in the content. Were you able to listen to a tape recording of a conversation between yourself and Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you listened -- did you listen to the actual recording, not the -- you were shown the transcript as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Were you able to say that it was your voice and that of Mico Stanisic to the investigator who was with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His voice for sure and mine, and mine, in places where I can hear that well. I'm not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Thank you very much. Then was there a second -- another conversation that took place, the number is 3231, between you and Momcilo Mandic? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember just -- well, that recording is not the best, there is some sort of interference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, agreed. But having listened to a conversation with a transcript that was said to be between you and Mr. Mandic, are you able to confirm that you did have such a conversation? That it was Mr. Mandic's voice on the tape and yours?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The recording is not good, but at some points I do hear myself and him thus at some points. But I cannot recall that conversation now when you are asking me -- when you ask me, do I recall that conversation, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But you're able -- all, as I said, I'm interested in the moment is your voices. Did you also listen to tapes, first of all, with the number 3237 where you had a conversation with Milenko Karisik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And there was one tape where the quality was, I agree, absolutely appalling. We enhanced it, sort of. And I just want -- we are going to try --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours, we got the papers, we didn't have an opportunity to play it to him because he already started giving evidence. I'd like you to listen to at lease part of it, which hopefully through the earphones you can make out some portions. And it's in sanction, sorry. The number of this one is 3238.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you able to -- Mr. Djeric, are you able to identify the voice there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mean you didn't hear it being played through the earphones at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a bad recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. One could -- some of us may think that one could hear a voice even through the terrible background noise. Did you hear that voice?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If Your Honours don't mind, we'll just try one more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't -- this -- I can't actually -- this is a bad recording. I can't follow that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you may not be able to follow it, but I'm asking you, whether however bad the recording, it may have seemed to some people that you could distinctly hear two different voices. Were you able to recognise either voice?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There is a lot of background noise, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I don't want to waste any more time on that. So you are able to identify the call between you and Mico Stanisic, the call between you and -- your voices, and Momcilo Mandic, and one call between you and Mr. Karisik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but you know, though, the one that you have just played back to me was really bad, so I can't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, leave aside that one. All of these calls, I mean, that's the only thing I want to ask you about, seem to have taken place between you and the Vraca school. Can you explain to the Court why you were getting in touch with people at the Vraca school?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, at that time I was a member of the leadership, and you may have noticed that they often requested the leadership, or rather the officials in Pale, and they didn't find them because they were tending to their own business because -- and I would be there because I was dealing with the operative tasks, and then they would find me. And when they say they want to communicate and they say we want to talk to you, they don't mean me, but one of us. They don't mean me expressly, but just one of us, and then they put me through to them. In one of the conversations, I was the one who wanted to talk to Stanisic because I was interested in what was going on down there. That's why I asked you about the date because I was not clear about the date. The date was not clear. It seems to me that that conversation took place immediately after the entry of the Serbian police into the MUP building in Vraca. I wasn't there when that happened. It's very important to know that the police entered the premises of the MUP in Vraca on the 4th of April, I suppose. And I was in Banja Luka at a meeting. I returned on the 5th, I believe. On the 5th of April I would say. And that conversation could have taken place at that time. Judging by everything, it could have been at that time because I arrived, and I inquired as to what was going on, and so on and so forth. So I am not very clear from the conversation which two people are in question. I know for one -- I know about one vice-president who is mentioned in the conversation, but as for the other two, I don't know whether I had Karadzic and Krajisnik in mind or somebody else. I really can't identify that. I arrived, I found the situation as it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Stop for a minute.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, he is actually going to the content, and to make sense of it, I mean, I think I better have it up on the screen. Presumably you are overruling Mr. Zecevic's objection to any discussion of the content?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, clearly the witness is questioning the contents of it, so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He is not questioning, he is talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but he is questioning the date when it was taken, so it's not this date which is on the document. That is exactly my -- the point why we are objecting to these intercepts, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I'm asking is whether -- the fact that he is querying the date is neither here nor there, it's the content that he is now referring to. But in any event, Your Honour, I think I'll move on because I've still got some other classes of documents to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, all I want to know about this is, were you aware in advance, even though you were in Banja Luka and not in Sarajevo, that the police school was going to be taken over by Mico Stanisic and Momcilo Mandic, amongst others? Before it happened, did you know about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. I didn't know. And the best argument to corroborate that is that I left my apartment and everything in the apartment. My car was in the garage. If I had known, I would have evacuated some of my belongings, the ones that could be moved. I didn't know because after that I never returned to my apartment, the one that I resided in before that. And this is the best proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave the question of the intercepts please, and can we have a look at one of the meetings which was a joint NSC Presidency meeting 1171, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is dated the 10th of May. Very briefly, Mr. Djeric, why had the National Security Council and the government joined together in a meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained yesterday, what the regime of one party means and what the government in that regime means, the party leadership, or rather, the president of the party and the president of the council for national security invited people from the government, as many as there were at the time, to that meeting. That was more of a coordinating -- I don't know how to put it, but it all boiled down to coordination. I apologise, yesterday I explained that the government was, as it were, within the regime of that party just a token government, like a toolbox. If a minister was needed to do a professional job, then he was taken like one would take a piece of -- a tool from that box, and that would be that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you say it was a token government. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the power was in the hands of the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which means that he was the power. You saw yesterday that even those members of the Presidency that were supposed to do their jobs didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just briefly look at this meeting then. This is on the 10th of May, and what is decided there, I think we can see from the first session, it was decided that the assembly session be held on the 12th of May in Banja Luka, and then the agenda, and then item number 5 was to be the decision on the take-over of soldiers of the JNA Yugoslav People's Army by the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of BH. And so can we summarise this meeting as deciding what was going to happen at this agenda -- I am sorry, at the 12th of May assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I don't remember what the objective of the meeting was, why it was called, and so on and so forth. It was simply at a time when the council for national security, which means the president, play the main role, and so on and so forth. And he was the one who run things. And I can't remember the details really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim that this was a preparatory meeting for an assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying you can't claim?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, you are asking me whether this has anything to do with the events that would transpire later, that will follow. I really can't remember what was discussed at the time in what spirit, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll give you a moment to read through the document again, Mr. Djeric, but isn't this setting the agenda for the 12th of May assembly, this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a lot of issues were raised and motions tabled, and Krajisnik was a member of that body as the president of the assembly. He may have tabled some of his agenda also.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were the prime minister of this government by then, weren't you, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually I was, I mean, well, there's no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government had been established, the ministers had already taken their positions. That's not in dispute. But I wasn't the one who prepared the assembly, I just participated in the preparations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was this meeting a preparation for the 12th of May assembly where one of the most important decisions was to create the Army of the Serbian Republic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But as I'm looking at the document, as I'm looking at the minutes, I would say that it turns out to be that way, but I'm saying that from just looking at the minutes I don't remember the session itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move then to the Presidency, please, meetings, just a selection. 1227 which I think will be the last document before the break, and which may answer the question that Judge Delvoie put yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday by Judge Delvoie about the Presidency and Dr. Karadzic. On the 31st of May, the second session of the Presidency was held, attended by Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Plavsic, Dr. Koljevic, and Momcilo Krajisnik -- sorry, I've got the wrong one. No, that's right. The session was chaired by Dr. Karadzic, the president of the Presidency. I have got the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see my name here. I'm not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, sorry. I've got the wrong one. You aren't the one that I want.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in fact, can we take the break so I can drag up the right one which is the one that I wanted. It's the first one of the 12th of May, and I just made a wrong note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've asked that 1226, I was one digit out, is put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is, in fact, the minutes of the first session of the Presidency on the 12th of May, so it's held -- indeed it says it was held after the assembly, in addition to the the members of the Presidency, the session was attended by Krajisnik and yourself, and we see the last line: "Member of the Presidency, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, was unanimously elected the president of the Presidency." And you were there for that, weren't you, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember this. I remember that there came a point in time when he was elected, but I can't remember that it was right here. I can't remember. Well, he was elected somewhat later as the president of the Presidency. I believe it was at an assembly session, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Djeric, you are looking at a document signed by Karadzic, Plavsic, and Koljevic, aren't you, that says that day, the 12th of May, after the assembly, he was elected?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I mean, I simply -- well, I don't remember this session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the president of the Presidency to be elected after an assembly session, well, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is the problem with him being elected after the assembly session?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I simply don't remember. That's why this is a bit -- I can't establish any links. Why should Karadzic and Plavsic sign, or rather, Koljevic, put his signature here, why should they do that? As members of a Presidency where Karadzic was president, I don't remember that. I remember that at a later assembly session, and I believe that there is a video recording of that, that he was -- that his candidacy was put up and that he was elected by a wider audience. I really don't understand. I don't remember when a two-member Presidency was transformed into a three-member Presidency. I simply can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Yes. Let's look at a couple of other meetings of the Presidency when you were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at 1229, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the 9th of June, at which time the Presidency is calling itself the War Presidency. Present was you and indeed General Mladic, General Gvero, and Colonel Tolimir. I think this is the first time we've come across Colonel Tolimir. Can you tell us who Colonel Tolimir was.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went along with the Commander Mladic, although he was a security officer, a military security officer. He was a member of the military security, but the two always went together. I know as much. And War Presidency, to be very honest, I don't understand the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about whether it's a War Presidency. I just want to deal with two matters on this meeting. "General Gvero reported on the situation in the area of the Banja Luka Corps and proposed that the authorities be established at all levels swiftly because of the widespread crimes." Do you remember if he expanded on what widespread crimes were being committed in Banja Luka or in the Banja Luka area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was a long time ago. In any case that was his job. He was some sort of a political factor within the army, so the story went together with him. And he often said that, however, within the context of this particular session, I can't remember that that was the case. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally on this document, item number 10 and 11, items: "Decision that the strategic goals and the map of Serbia BH and representations to the European community be published," and, "Instruct members of the Serbian army to abide by the Geneva Conventions in their treatment of the prisoners of war." And we see it's signed, don't we, by Dr. Karadzic as president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1243, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the 13th of June, so four days after the last meeting. Again you are present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we look, please, at the second page of the English and the second page of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item number 4, conclusion was adopted that the ministry of the Interior of Serbia and Montenegro, ministries of the interior, be requested to conduct investigations into the purchasing and selling of all Gulf cars of Vogosca make and other products of the TSA factory which occurred on the territory of those republics in the last three months. Can I deal just deal with this very quickly because it's going to come up in other contexts. There was a scandal, was there not, about the thefts of Volkswagens from this particular factory Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then item number 8. Which I think we need to go to the third page of the B/C/S. It's on the second pages -- same pages. Under 2: "Urgently activate the work of the commission for war crimes committed against the Serbian people of BH." So do you remember you were answering questions earlier when the commission was established, it's clear, isn't it, from this, Mr. Djeric, that this was a commission to investigate crimes against Serbs, and nobody else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I mean when we spoke about crimes we meant all crimes. And you will see that I'm talking about myself, about the government, about government meetings. This was always discussed at government meetings, and relevant ministries were tasked with reporting on the security of people and their property irrespective of their ethnicity and to prosecute those who committed crimes against people. That was the position of the government, the conclusion of the government, and of the commission. In this specific case, I simply believe that this does not reflect to the largest possible extent the spirit of our efforts, well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... If that's what you say let's have a look at --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which means that all I'm saying is that this conclusion, if you compared this with the conclusions of the government, you would see discrepancies, you would see differences in the sense of the words that I'm saying. We were talking about the -- persecuting all crimes including crimes committed against other peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In that event, let's have a look at one more out of this selection of documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 931. We are moving to the 6th of August now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again a meeting which you were present, and if we go to page 2 in the English and page 2 also in the B/C/S. Where in this meeting, Mr. Djeric, you actually discussed the work of the commission for investigating war crimes committed against the Serbian people. Now, are you saying that was discussing crimes committed against Muslims and Croats as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the policies that we pursued at the time. I'm talking about the government, and so on and so forth. You can't see from this what crimes are being discussed, were they the crimes against people in Sarajevo. I can't see it from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You can't see what from here? All right. And indeed at this meeting, just to remind you, this was just after, wasn't it, the camps in the Prijedor area had been brought to public attention by the international media because that's what the last part of this meeting was discussing, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't recall that. I don't recall what was discussed, whether that was discussed at all. I really can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Djeric, just have a look at the last part of this document which talks about the treatment of what is described as prisoners of war and then the conclusion that the Ministry of the Interior "... will be ordered to examine through its municipal branches the behaviour of all civilian authorities and individuals guarding prisoners of war. The information will be passed to the MUP which will pass it on to the Presidency..."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the practice. That was the practice to issue orders to the MUP and the Ministry of Justice to have the information to submit reports to the authorised bodies. That was the practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what the Presidency was ordering, that Mico Stanisic investigate and report to it, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency and the government asked for regular reports, and you can see that in the minutes of meetings of the government and in the records of their meetings that such reports were requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, we are going to look at a couple of the government meeting minutes in a minute. But this was an actual order, wasn't it, that the Presidency wanted to find out what was going on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is in the domain of Karadzic because he has the jurisdiction over the MUP, the military, so this would have the indications of an order. He frequently mixed those up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you had jurisdiction, you've explained this to us yesterday, over the MUP, or the minister was obliged to report to you over non-military matters?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain segments MUP would be responsible to the government in the cases of budget, certain issues, judicial matters. It should have been like that, but most often this didn't occur. That wasn't the case. Because the minister believed that he had more connection to the president.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at a couple of examples, please, of the meetings that you held as the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, 1180, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, can I ask as long as this document is still up to the witness, Mr. Djeric, on this commission of -- for investigation war crimes, there was only one commission for investigation -- investigating war crimes, wasn't there? There was not a second one? There was only one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one. One commission that was dealing with this matter, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the name of that commission was the commission for investigating war crimes committed against the Serbian people; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that that is what it was called, but it did encompass other problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have 1180 now on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a government meeting of the 31st of May. If we go to the last page in each just to confirm that it's your typewritten signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we now go back, please, to the 5th page in English and the third page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item 15: "The Ministry of the Interior has informed the government about the current issues in the political and security situation in the republic, about the degree of public order and peace and about other issues of importance for safety in the republic. Regarding this issue, it had been concluded that the government is not sufficiently informed about the issues relevant to its work, especially about the situation in the front. It has been concluded that the government must be regularly informed about the said issues through the Defence, Main Staff, and Ministry of Interior in order to be able, within its rights and authority, engage into formulating policy and attitudes coming up with appropriate solutions and their realisation." Now, does that accurately reflect what your view as president of the government was, was the role of the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that what is written here is written in the sense that we did really in a certain way express our dissatisfaction because we had been marginalised, pushed to the side. We didn't have any information about anything. In order to do anything, you need to have the information and you need to know. So we did place this particular question on the agenda several times, several times, but the focus of the authorities was around the president, and I hope that I clarified that. It's the regime of one party, that's what the situation was. The president had the cadre suggestions and solutions, the influence lay with the president, and so on and so forth. We asked to be informed, to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. You've answered the question, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll look at one more on this aspects of information, 1183, please, which is the 3rd of June. And can we go to the third page in the B/C/S and the third page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There we see under item number 2: "The report of the work -- about the work of the National Security Service should be prepared and submitted to the government for adopting - responsible: The Ministry of Interior." And again we are back to war crimes. "A procedure for determining war crimes should be initiated - responsible. The Ministry of Interior and the committee for war crimes..." I want to ask you about a meeting in -- on the 18th of June, which is 1192. 16th of June, you are presiding. The deputy prime minister, Mr. Grubojevic [phoen] is there. You who else is there. Also present, secretary of the governor. And Slobodan Skipina standing in for Mico Stanisic. Now how often did it happen that somebody stood in for Stanisic at your meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened often. Especially after July when there were certain disagreements and a certain conflict between myself and my colleague the minister, Mr. Stanisic. Especially from July onwards, he simply didn't appear at the government meetings; he would always be sending someone. For example, there would be 15 meetings that would be held, and there would only be attendance at one or two occasions. He kept justifying himself that he was on some other assignments and so on, but he simply wasn't there. He was just ignoring the government.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are finding it difficult to hear the witness because of background noise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just look, please, at item 8 which is on the fourth page in the English and fourth page in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The government took notice of the letter by the Sarajevo corps command related to, among other things, problems with the functioning of the civilian authorities in the municipalities." What was the problems with the functioning of civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't see that text. Oh, yes, there it is. For the most part, the military would come with certain remarks that they had problems with the municipalities, and so on and so forth, that the communication wasn't well, that they were not working enough, that they were not active enough. And then you would always have a mention of crimes there, so in that case, I mean, I guess there was a bit of distrust and so on. They always complained about one another. They would be the civilian authorities coming from the municipalities complaining about the military; the military would be complaining about the civilian authorities. This is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two other documents, and then we'll move to the final, as it were, the ending of your Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1199, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the 9th of July. We can see again that again Mico Stanisic isn't present, but sends somebody called Pero Vujicic. Can we go, please, to item number 8, page 4 of the English and page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 4, please, item 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The question has been raised whether there are agreed criteria regarding the moving out of the Muslim population from the territory in the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It has been concluded the government has not until now had a point of view on this matter. "The Ministry of the Interior is entrusted with preparing information on this issue that the government would consider and take the appropriate standpoint." Okay, Mr. Djeric, what criteria for the of moving out of the population?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think somebody posed this question that had to do with some kind of moving out voluntarily, if they wanted to move to a different territory for security reasons. I assume that this question was put and then the reply was that we don't have a position on that, nor did we discuss that, nor was something like that asked of us. So somebody put that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But why was the minister of the interior supposed to deal with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply, the ministry of Internal Affairs had the power, let me put it that way, it had its people out in the field. This was an operational ministry, operative ministry that could inform us what was going on in the field. I wasn't able to know what was going on throughout the whole territory, which in any case was subject to migration and, you know, voluntarily -- voluntary migrations, forced ones due to fear. The ministry was asked to prepare information about what was the situation in the field, what was happening out in the field, so that we could have the information. It was not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it was voluntary moving out by the Muslims as opposed to forced moving them out, why would that involve the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not a question of a role. What was being asked here was information. We didn't have control over the territory, so in that sense information was sought from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But why couldn't the government seek information from the political leadership in the various territories as to the voluntary nature of this moving out by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this is the time of tectonics, so we didn't have any contact with the territory. The territory was not integrated. You couldn't reach the territory often. You had enclaves often, and besides that, that part of the party, the party aspect of it, you still had the Serbian autonomous provinces functioning still. They were not abolished at that time. So you had a parallelism of power. You had the power, and then you had these autonomous regions which were functioning by themselves in their own way, and they also had the power and the authority. The government did not have full effective power here, and we were trying to get to some information, specific information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean please by tectonics?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean simply is that the strings had snapped, you understand, the former state that existed before didn't exist, all the strings had snapped. The enclaves were formed on all sides. You had several territories which were separate, isolated islands, you didn't know what was going on. So we didn't have access to those areas. Perhaps you could reach somebody by helicopter in some way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but you did have assembly meetings, didn't you, in this period? If fact we are going to look at one from the 23rd of July, so why couldn't this have been discussed with the deputies to the assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the assembly there was a certain agenda and then, amongst other things, the functioning would be discussed at the assembly as well. The functioning of the power. No assembly passed without this being discussed. And it was noted that there were problems and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a look, as I say, at the 23rd of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then one last document from the government minutes, 28th of July; 1211, please. Page 2 -- sorry, not page 2. Page 4 in the English and -- sorry, I've lost it. For some reason I don't seem to have marked it in the B/C/S. I'm sorry, what did I say? No, page 4 in English, I want. I see now, yes, at the top, yes. I have marked it, sorry, it's page 4 in the B/C/S as well. Second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's you, Mr. Djeric, reminding the cabinet ministers of their obligations to attend government sessions, emphasising it's unacceptable that some ministers have attend only one or two out of the 14 government sessions held in the last two months. Who did you have in mind when you were reminding them of it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all the minister of Internal Affairs, Mr. Stanisic, that is him, but then there's also Mandic. First of all the two of them because they liked to be with the president to spend time with him and so on, and he also believed that the minister of Internal Affairs of justice, the defence ministers, all, that their place was with him, he thought that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I am sorry, there is one last one because it reflects, I think, what you've been talking about. 1506, please, which is handwritten notes. We need to go to the second page in B/C/S, and the first page in English. Sorry, third page in B/C/S. It's just the cover of the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, this is a handwritten record of the meeting that was apparently held on the 14th of September in Bijeljina. Do you know who wrote those minutes? Do you recognise the writing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, in the English to fifth page, and in the B/C/S to the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trbojevic is saying there's a government crisis, and he is at item number 5: "The law on internal affairs is in a similar way. The minister is tied to the Presidency, and the government has no influence." It goes on to say: "We have not succeeded in gaining sovereignty, because we have not taken control over the territory." Then Mr. Subotic, the minister of defence speaks, and can with question down to the bottom, please, of the first page. Stanisic replies, saying, Mr. Trbojevic speaks improperly of the police, we have more than a thousand reports, the law was adopted, we reassigned assistants. And then the MUP is being used as an organ for exercising power. Do you remember this meeting, when there appears to be a row between Mr. Trbojevic and Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the meeting, the particulars of it, but I do remember that at one point in time there was some difference of opinion between them, a quarrel, and so on and so forth. Because vice-president Trbojevic was coordinating internal policy; he was vice-president for internal policy. So the Ministry of the Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Justice were under his jurisdiction, and he was placed in a situation that he was unable to control those two ministers. When I say control, I mean to work with them simply. And what happened was that the government was already being informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Finally, Mr. Djeric, I want to look at briefly the minutes of the 23rd of July, the assembly there, which is 928, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 17th assembly, 17th session, which was held in Jahorina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several, many were held, I guess, I assume it was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I am sorry, do you remember this one in July?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the particulars, but I know that one was held in early 1992. When I say early, what I mean is in the middle, at Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was a lengthy speech from Mr. Karadzic and then you spoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's page 20, I hope, in the English, and page 18, I think, in the B/C/S. I don't know how it comes out in e-court, that's the trouble. It's page 19, is it? Okay, 19 in B/C/S. It would be 18, first, just so you can see his name. Can we have page 18 in the B/C/S and then page 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I tell you what, it's probably easier -- you've got to look at it as well if he has the binder. Right. Mr. Djeric -- I'm afraid I'm going to have to ask you to go to the next page. Do you see, you speak there. I just want going to ask you about something you say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the next page in each document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You're complaining about the running of the government, Mr. Djeric, and you say, you are drawing an analogy with children's diseases, and say about three quarters of the way down the page: "This refers primarily to the numerous flaws in the running of the judiciary, the interior affairs organ, and even government." What flaws were you trying to identify in the interior affairs organs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic weakness when it comes to the Ministry of Interior and I'm talking about the minister, is a poor coordination, poor coordination between myself and the minister. To put it simply, the minister ignored the government, or rather, he simply believed that he belonged to the president along the chain of command. And for him, the government was a secondary thing, and so on and so forth. And we could not work, of course, if we did not have an adequate insight into the work of the Ministry of the Interior. The key issue was coordination. The government could not operate without information. It could not manage control without information.
