We always sought information from the ground, from the municipalities, we always sought information that also implied certain proposals for measures, and we never received that, those things were discussed by the president and the Presidency, that was the major problem. And in addition to that, the minister was, you know, a bit rough around the edges, and he could be unpleasant, so that coordination was becoming more thwarted and made our job more difficult. And that's the main reason why he became more and more distanced from the government. I don't know if this is a good opportunity for me to talk about such things. I really -- we simply thought that the ministry was not working as well as it should, that it could be engaged to a larger extent down there, that they should cooperate with us, that we should do things together. The minister, to put it simply, started to live a role as a commander, his command function was more important to him than his function as the minister. And that was a big problem on his side. Well, I think that's enough from me on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is the assembly - I don't want to take you back to it because it takes so long to get to it - where Mr. Karadzic said that all of the territory that the Serbs had claimed was controlled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look at one thing that Ms. Plavsic said, which is on page 38 of the English; and it's 39, I think, of the B/C/S. Is that page 39? Can we maybe go back, please, sorry. Try 38, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a pause for a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if I could ask the Court Officer to give this binder to the witness, at least he can get to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to -- Your Honours, can I -- this is going to take too long otherwise, and he needs to look at the one where he resigned. But you've got in front of you, haven't you, Mr. Djeric, Mrs. Plavsic's speech. And did she say there: "Let me tell you immediately that I feel no difference should be made between the two" -- I'm sorry. "I will begin this topic with the relationship between the maps and the conquered territories. Let me tell you immediately that I feel that no difference should be made between these two concepts. 65 per cent of Serb territory belongs to our people according to the cadastre," whatever that may be, "and 70 per cent of the conquered one, which is only a 5 per cent gain in relation to the previous number." Now earlier today, you referred to the maps that had been drawn up for the Cutileiro agreement. Did you understand Mrs. Plavsic to be saying that the fact that more territory had been taken over than was originally envisioned by these maps didn't matter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I don't know what Mrs. Plavsic meant here. Especially in light of the fact that she socialised with officers because her role was also the role as a commander. I can only tell you that there was an opinion going around that 64 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina belonged to the Serbian people, judging by the maps and the zoning ordinances, and that was the starting point for all the negotiations. Maps were being drawn and all sorts of things like that. I can tell that you. But I don't know what she meant, I can't comment upon that. I don't know what territory was held, what the army held. I'm sure -- well, I would say that she was privy to some information or dealt with some information that I don't know anything of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page into each of, I think, the B/C/S and English because this bears on what we were talking about, in fact, one of your meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic also went on to say, didn't she, the following, which is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't read the English page, can we make the English page slightly bigger. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "We must be prepared to move large masses of people from place to place within our conquered territories in a short period for the sake of defensive activities. Unfortunately we can count on Serbia less and less which is already exhausted by receiving our refugees and those wounded, while it's also in a difficult situation. That is why we have to create conditions for domestic, military, and forced emigration, and we cannot do that without territories." Now, do you remember a few minutes ago, Mr. Djeric, we discussed the question of why Mico Stanisic had been made responsible for Muslims moving out, and you said it was because you couldn't talk to people about this -- the political leaders. Why couldn't have that been discussed at this session where Mrs. Plavsic is raising that question?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, okay, this is her opinion. She is thinking here the way she is thinking. But to put it simply, it's not -- it's her -- well, her opinion, and I don't think that it attracted much attention at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but, why didn't you at that stage say, Well, Mrs. Plavsic has raised this; we've discussed in the government what needs to be done. How should we cope with the Muslims who want to move out? What criteria should we adopt?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I simply -- I did not deem it important to intervene at every single meeting when somebody went off on a tangent. I didn't think it was necessary for me to say we had discuss that at our government meeting, and this is our conclusion. I didn't think it would be prudent for me to go against a member of the government. But what is important is that the government did things differently than Plavsic put -- made it believe. We tasked the Ministry of the Interior to brief us, to secure order down there, and these are some ideas voiced on the part of Biljana Plavsic, why don't you ask her about them? These are an individual's thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you to look at one more speech then by Mr. Prstojevic. It's page 68, I believe, in the B/C/S, and it's about -- it's 65 in the English. Can we just -- no, that's not -- sorry, 67 in the B/C/S. I thought it was one page ahead. Sorry, 67 in B/C/S. 67, please, not 68. My mistake. One page behind in the the B/C/S, please. Thank you. And in the English it's page 65. So whatever that page is, it's not the right one. Thank you, that's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, who Mr. Prstojevic is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prstojevic, I assume that you are talking about the chief of the municipality of Ilidza at the time. I suppose you're talking about Nedeljko Prstojevic because I don't see his -- if that's him, then -- well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It clearly is because it says he is being asked to speak by questions he is being asked by the citizens of Sarajevo. And he says the following: "Namely when the Serbs started the uprising in Sarajevo and when they seized control over certain territories, there was no government, or at least it was not known where it was then. More over, we did not even know Mr. Karadzic was alive during the first couple of days. When we learned that he was alive and when he visited us Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory, and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been a majority." Now, was that an accurate description, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I -- well, this is what he says. I don't know what was going on down there. He was the chief of that municipality, and he was also in charge of the municipal SDS, and he was also a member of the Crisis Staff. So they were the government, the authorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if that was correct that they had driven Muslims out of the municipalities in which they were a majority, Mr. Djeric, was that something of which you as the prime minister approved of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not approve anything, this is what I've been telling you all this time. Did I everything in my power to prevent that. The government arrived at conclusions to draw information and reports about the security of people and their property irrespective of their ethnic affiliation. Our position is clear, we did not support that. But those were party activities. The activities of the Crisis Staff. Prstojevic [realtime transcript read in error "Plavsic"] was also a member of the Crisis Staff. They were the power. You have to bear in mind, I would kindly ask you to bear in mind, that we tried to exert effective control. I even resigned and walked out because the government did not exert control over the territory, did not exert effective power in the proper sense of that word. But we tried hard, and it wasn't easy, believe me. We are talking about very complex problems, but we did try. We showed goodwill.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's all I'm going ask about that meeting. Finally the meeting where you resigned or your resignation was accepted, the 23rd and 24th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner, just transcript, page 50, line 24, it says Plavsic was also member of the Crisis Staff. He said Prstojevic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we finally look at the record of the meeting where you gave your explanation for resigning, 933. And your speech starts at page 642 in B/C/S. Page 11 in the B/C/S. And page 15 in the English. Right. And then we need to go on, please, in that to the next page in both the B/C/S and English. I'm sorry, Your Honours, I don't know why -- it's been photocopied with some highlighting obviously, I missed it when I was going through it the other day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you said first of all in that paragraph: "I will never be against changes in the government, but I will always be against the bullies in the government." Who were you referring to as the bullies in the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the two ministers, the minister of the interior, Mico Stanisic, and the minister of justice, Momcilo Mandic. I was referring to two individuals who simply ignored the work of the government, didn't keep in touch, did not do their jobs well. Rumour has it and I can't be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry about who you were referring to, that's all. So it was those two ministers again. And then you went on to say at the next page -- and you named the both of them - I didn't want to trouble you with that - but you had named the minister of justice and the minister of the Internal Affairs not coming to government sessions, only to the president of the republic or the president of the assembly. Stanisic responded to you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go, please, to page -- page 15 in the B/C/S, and page 19 and in the English. First of all just to see the beginning. You responded after Mandic had responded. And then can we go over to the next page in each English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He said, in the paragraph -- third paragraph in the B/C/S and in the English, he is referring to you, and he said: "I, of course, did not accept that. There are a lot of examples, and I emphasise here in front of you that I had followed a policy of the Presidency of the Serbian Democratic Party and our deputies in the former state and, I have always been in favour of the policy." From what you knew of Stanisic from the time that you began working with him, was that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I mean, I did not know Stanisic well. I knew him superficially, but I didn't know whether he was a competent, whether he could do the job. The party was looking for somebody, Karadzic insisted on the names, Stanisic Buha. Stanisic's candidacy put up; he was accepted. I don't know what he was like. I don't know anything about his productivity. I can't talk about that. He -- well, you know, I don't know how he worked as a member of the party because I'm not a party member.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djeric, that's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, am I right to understand that you finally decided to resign from the government because of the fact that you were unable to control these two ministers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Please, bear in mind this: I did not resign in late October. I did resign in late October; it was accepted in November. But the problems were put on the agenda even before that. First at the government sessions in August and then that discussion spilled over and reached a political leadership, but I could not receive the green light for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, please listen the question that I'm putting to you. The question is the following: Did you choose to resign from the government because you felt at the time that you were unable to control ministers Stanisic and Mandic? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, yes, yes. I first asked for their resignation two or three months before I asked from the political leadership to remove those two men. But they wouldn't do that. They wouldn't accept that. And that's the long and the short of it, and the government was paralysed, without the Ministry of the Interior, and just as the government could not operate. And in addition to that, Mr. Stanisic is rough around the edges. There is a lot to be desired in the area of communication and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So you did try to get rid of them and when you discovered that you could not throw them out of the government, you chose to leave the government instead; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did everything in my power for them to be removed and replaced. Not only them, but primarily them. There were some other personnel issues, and changes had it to be carried out in the echelons of the power because the crime -- criminal activities escalated and paralyzed the power. I wanted to do it already a few months before, but I never -- my agenda never reached the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, are you -- Mr. Cvijetic, you will cross -- are you ready to begin? You have five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we start, or shall we take a break to provide for some continuity in my cross-examination, Your Honours? I'm in your hands. Maybe the five minutes will spoil the context of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we can shift the break by five minutes. It means we are coming back five minutes early. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I am Slobodan Cvijetic representing Mr. Stanisic as co-counsel. Before I start putting questions to you about your testimony, I'm going to ask you, and this applies to me as well, to pay attention to this technical problem that we can make together. We speak the same language actually, and it's happened to me very often that I start talking with the witness and that I forget that all of that has to be interpreted by the interpreters. So when I finish my question, could you please make a short break and you can follow on the screen when the cursor stops, indicating that the translation is complete. So that way we can then make sure that all is in the transcript and that the Trial Chamber and the interpreters do not have to warn us to slow down or make a break. So let's begin. You were a member of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a member of the ministerial council of Republika Srpska, and prime minister designate, and then the prime minister of the government Republika Srpska. So you were at the very top as events were unfolding in the period that is relevant to this indictment, or these proceedings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with you that I was at the top because events there were focused at the top of the parties or between or among the parties, and so a lot of things were happening there, and not in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time or at the ministerial council of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. But in any case you were in those bodies, this is not something at that is contested?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you also are a university professor, an economist, and in view of that fact as well as what I said earlier, whether you wished so or not, you are suitable as a witness for me through to you try to present and get an idea of the situation in which you took over the responsibilities you took over in the government of Republika Srpska for Republika Srpska. So I'm going to begin from the period when the generating of the crisis in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina began. You would agree with me, Mr. Djeric, that the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for decades following World War II built and achieved a system practically in all spheres which was - you are an economist, you will understand - complimentary, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a system that had its problems, I don't know what you are thinking of when you say complimentary. There was some inter-independency [as interpreted], that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the system had problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you changed the word that it was interlinked and interdependent, and this is precisely what I was thinking of. No single federal unit had everything it needed in order to be autonomous.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it should have been, but not all the the federal units were in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, that is exactly what I'm saying. This was done through administrative measures and some where the natural resources didn't permit or allow a federal unit to be absolutely independent from all the others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, simply as a rule, no one was able to exist unto themselves, but that was another reason, and that later turned out to be true with some federal units, that they were able to secede and continue an independent life with the assistance of external economic aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you will agree that the cessation of one part -- with the cessation of one part of the former Yugoslavia, the whole system was disrupted, it wasn't any more a single system?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was disrupted. It ceased to exist as a single system. I said that yesterday. Separatism on behalf of certain republics led to the crisis overall and to the existential fear that was felt among all of us in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, you have answered my nest question, thus, that's what happened. Actually the separatism of Slovenia followed by that of Croatia began to destroy the singleness of that system.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and Bosniaks, as a people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I haven't entered Bosnia yet. So we have agreed, Slovenia is leaving -- Croatia is leaving, the whole system is collapsing. And then two troubles arrive at the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I can put it that way. First of all, the unified single system was disrupted in all spheres. I don't have to go into all of them, but beginning from the economy, the transportation system, culture, tourism, and so on. And then there is a second trouble that arrives at the borders, and this is the war in the neighbouring Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot be immune and keep itself separate from all of those problems which are going to enter its territory.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fate that met the former Yugoslavia, one could not expect Bosnia-Herzegovina to avoid that fate because it was Yugoslavia in miniature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to put some questions which are going to indicate what the situation was in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, other than these external factors, Bosnia and Herzegovina had its own internal problems; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I would begin from political problems. Following multiparty elections, new power was elected and constituted which followed upon the previous communist one; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The mainly nationalist parties came into power; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So they jointly worked together in the period when they needed to defeat communism; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's when they cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Then after that goal was achieved, some secret plans of some parties began to come to light leading to the implementation of some other goals; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was evident especially in terms of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You are thinking of the party of democratic action which represented the interests of the Muslim people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I think in your testimony you said that you pointed to two events which you believed generated the crisis and led to the government that you were at the head of becomes a practically wartime government instead of working normally in peacetime conditions. Just one second. Well, you can answer now.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday I particularly emphasised that we hoped and expected that we are going to have full control over processes and that the government would rule in a normal manner like a peacetime government. But this was disrupted primarily by two events, which I'm going to refer to once again. And that is the failure of the Cutileiro plan and particularly, particularly, particularly -- well, this first plan -- there was a plan, then it fails; then there's another plan, and so on. But in particular in this sense an event that had a particularly negative effect was the attack on the army in the Tuzla airport, and so on. This came as a shock. And also I am not overlooking the referendum which at that time was the most burning problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, when you refer to that, tell us which referendum specifically you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the referendum conducted in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 1st of March, 1992, about the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on which two ethnic groups voted because the referendum was organised in such a way that two ethnic groups could vote to the detriment of the third one, even though such a referendum could not have been organised from the point of view of the constitution. So this is a referendum that was not constitutional. All people should have been consulted. So after these two events, everything that followed after that was a consequence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since in the transcript it does not say what you said, and that that is that it was a forceful violent act, I'm going to say that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is what I meant, that it was a forceful violent act in terms of the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, let us wait for it to be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I really don't think that Mr. Cvijetic ought to tell him what he said. He should ask him again what he said. Your Honours, it's line 20 through to 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I needn't return Ms. Korner's point, it's obvious. It's a recurrent problem, which we visited before. But when the witness is asked to clarify -- well, in this case, although he is -- the transcript says that that is what he meant, but could you for the sake of accuracy ask the question again and get the answer from the witness in terms of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the problem is very simple. I'm going to say it. A part of the witness's answer was not entered in the transcript. Mr. Djeric said it was a violent act. All I wanted to know -- the question was what sort of violence was he thinking of? That is -- here it is; that's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to clarify. I explained that yesterday, and I'm going to do it again today. It's a question of violating the constitution. A referendum was carried out in a way that was not provided for under the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well, I think we've covered that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was an unconstitutional act.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to have to take you back to another event from 1991, and that is the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was convened on the 15th of October, 1991, I think. Do you know about that assembly session?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Perhaps I was there. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to remind you, in that assembly session a decision was reached on the declaration or proclamation of the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, do you remember it now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, I mean, details. I know this was spoken about and this was the time of those events and happenings, but as for which assembly session adopted which document, and so on...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right, I'm going to tell you. It's the assembly session following which the Serbian deputies left the session because they did not wish to participate and give legitimacy to the voting of such a decision. Do you remember it now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So I cannot but not ask you whether you perhaps attended this assembly session.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really say whether I actually was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. But can you at least confirm for me whether you were a member of the government at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the government. I should have attended by virtue of that, but I don't really remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to remind you that assembly was -- let me put it that way, was covered from the perspective of the media very well. And very often in the media and here also in all the opening statements in the cases before this Tribunal, the address of the then president of the Serbian Democratic Party Mr. Radovan Karadzic is referred to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that? Do you remember that address of his?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what address you mean. If you are thinking about the address when he said that is that, you know, one of those statements of his concern about events, the disappearance of the people, isn't it, and so on and so forth, yes, I didn't attend that meeting. I definitely did not attend that meeting, but I don't [as interpreted] know that I watched that on the television screen, but -- on the television, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you watched the session on television?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very often from the context of that address, one sentence is taken out. He is addressing the MPs of the Croatian democratic union and the SDA, the party of democratic action. And this particular sentence is often singled out: "Don't think that you will not take Bosnia and Herzegovina into the hell and the Muslim people into an oblivion, because the Muslim people cannot defend themselves from a war should it take place here." So you will agree with me that that sentence has been articulated many times in the media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, it has been taken out of the context of a very broad discussion. And then this was done to give that sense the character of a threat. Let me rewind a little bit and quote Mr. Karadzic who says: "Gentlemen, I assure you, firstly, even if you took a decision this evening, but there's no way for you to take that decision, because we have constitutional ways to prevent you from taking a vote. Even if you did vote and took a decision, that would be a shame for Mr. Izetbegovic in The Hague because we have a way to prevent that from taking place, from that happening in The Hague." Do you agree with me that Mr. Karadzic as a matter of fact, issues a threat by resorting to a constitutional means to prevent a decision from being taken?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a conclusion that can be arrived at, and that's clear. And it is also clear that he is concerned about Bosnia-Herzegovina, although he says that Mr. Karadzic -- Mr. Karadzic used to say things in a haste without really thinking, not speaking as a politician should. It shouldn't have [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you a few more sentences before we bring this matter to an end. "I implore with you - once again, I'm not threatening, I'm imploring - that you should understand the interpretation of the political will of the Serbian people seriously. They are here being represented by the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian renewal movement and some other Serbs belonging to some other parties, please understand the situation seriously. What you are doing is not good. The road to which you want to take Bosnia and Herzegovina is the same highway to hell and hardships that Slovenia and Croatia had opted for and have taken before you." You will agree with me, won't you, that this could be a benevolent way to draw everybody's attention to the perils of such a decision?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see I've already spoken about this existential fear and the concern of the Serbian people and its leadership about the further destiny of Bosnia. Bosnia within the framework of Yugoslavia is one thing, and Bosnia as an independent state is a different thing. At that moment, the leadership were trying to make an effort to pull the three people's together and organise Bosnia and Herzegovina but not at the detriment of any other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me give you one more sentence, and we will arrive at the same conclusion as you did. Further on Mr. Karadzic says as follows: "From now on, gentlemen, until the moment you remove the issue of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the table, from the agenda, I will take the floor regularly. It's my right." Mr. Djeric, you know from your own parliamentary practice that sometimes speakers when they want to obstruct a process of decision-making behave by abusing their right to a limitless number of appearances, and time for discussion given to them. And that Mr. Karadzic, as it were, resorted to that last means to prevent a decision from being taken by announcing that he would not stop talking.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say to you. I don't know what to say. He behaved the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Anyway, be it as it may, the decision on the declaration of independence was taken without the consent of one of the three constituent peoples; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was that decision entire anti-constitutional, could it have been taken at the detriment of another people, with that one people's vital interest being threatened by that decision?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the constitution imposed a consensus when it came to taking such decisions. All three peoples had to be in consent pursuant to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. However, if that consensus on such an important issue as was the organisation of a future state was not reached, what would have been an available alternative?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If the three peoples could not reach a consensus on such an important issue, what was the alternative?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The alternative was chaos, disorder, problems, and so on and so forth. That was the alternative. The situation that couldn't be controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't want to tell you who it was, but one witness told us what followed was a divorce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw. I withdraw my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Strike that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, war did not take place after the assembly session; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What happened was peace negotiations under the auspices of the European community with the mediation of the Portuguese diplomat Mr. Cutileiro; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The peace talks or negotiations about the constitutional principles of the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina were successful by the signatories putting their initials on those constitutional principles?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: According to those constitutional principles, Bosnia and Herzegovina persisted as an international subject and as an independent and sovereign state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was accepted by all the three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. However, it's internal organisation envisaged the protection of the vital interests of the three constituent peoples within the Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphone and could all the unnecessary microphones please be switched off, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The authorities that the entities or cantonal units, or whatever they were called according to the plan at the time, would have?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The first part of the question was missed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was envisaged by the plan and some solutions were proposed by that plan as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you've already mentioned that in practice a process started to implement those constitutional principles that were initialled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Every side in the spirit of that document and that plan started to build whatever was planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And what was planned there was for the entities to have their own governments and their own ministries; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the details of the document. I know that there were some functions, some organs, and so on and so forth, and everything else that a state should have. Some fundamental things were offered in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Amongst other things, what was offered was the alienation in certain spheres of government which were not entrusted to Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that plan was based on regionalisation, decentralisation of the state, and provided for some functions to be given to those decentralised units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic withdrew his initial from that plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, this happened, I really can't say when, after how long. First the plan was adopted and initialled, and subsequently the Bosniak side and Mr. Izetbegovic withdrew their consent and gave up on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then you'll have to agree with me that the previous decision taken on the part of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina about the declaration of sovereignty which was taken on the 15th or the 16th October, 1991, could have been the first or the initial generator of the political crisis that struck Bosnia and Herzegovina after that time. And as you've already told us, everything else what happened was just a consequence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to anticipate what could have or should have or might have happened. In any case, that date, the date of that assembly and the way it ended and what it concluded about the sovereignty was the cross-roads for everything else that happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And after all that, the things that you are talking about, this second point in time for which you say is very important, and that is the rejection of Cutileiro's plan and the attack on the JNA column?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the two points in time which simply had an impact on the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and put it in a very dire position. Those were the events that resulted in a state of chaos without any control.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the Court please produce a document. 1D00-3812. Your Honours, it is a set of documents, therefore, I would ask you to allow me to provide the hard copies to Mr. Djeric, which would make his life easier. He would not have to refer to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I think that we need to -- the first question he is being asked is whether the witness has ever seen this document before or knows anything about the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this will determine whether I tender this document or not, but that does not exclude my right to discuss the document with him; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As long as we can also follow what is going on, because we need to see the document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say that the document you are showing now is just one of a bundle?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and we will be going through the pages, we'll take them one at a time. They are all connected. And you will see on the screen the same documents that the witness will be looking at. May I, please, be allowed to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, is this document on your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I can't find it. It's 3815.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What is on the transcript is 381.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, do you have the first document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you understand what this is all about? The minister --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, I am sorry, before he can start making comments which will effectively [indiscernible], the first question must be, has the witness ever seen this document before; second, if he hasn't, does he know anything about the contents. Otherwise it's just pure comment that's going to be made by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to be given an opportunity to put my questions to the witness. I've not had an opportunity to put those questions to the witness, have I?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I'm not going to ask you about the document. I will start by asking you something else.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not seen the document before to get that out of the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina took a decision about the withdrawal of the JNA units from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you know about that in principle?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did hear about the decision, I was taken to that effect. I heard that they did take the decision about the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. And this is the decision on page 1, you will see the accompanying letter by the Ministry of Defence Mr. Jerko Doko. And could we please go immediately to the following page, and here you can see the decision on the following page, the decision follows. Can you see that? So you know about this decision. You probably didn't have the opportunity to see the text, at least that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't see the document, the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina worked on this which was headed by minister Jerko Doko.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: One more thing. Was Minister Doko minister at the same time as you were in the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the next document in this package, 1D00-2795.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's the document that follows immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S, it's the bottom part. And that's the part with the signature, so we'll have to go forward with the English version. We need to look at item marked 4, so we will have to look at the next page in the English. All right. This is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, do you see whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who was Alija Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the minister of Internal Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was he also a member of the government that you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 of his order, it says, literally: "Planning and launching of combat activities throughout the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is to be accomplished as soon as possible and coordinated with the Territorial Defence staff of the region, district, and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." The order in the heading refers to the decision of the Presidency ordering the withdrawal of the JNA units. However, Mr. Djeric, you can see from paragraph 4 that the army will be -- will not be permitted to leave peacefully, but an attack is being planned on the military columns.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order is clear, and it says to plan quickly and launch activities, military activities, so you cannot conclude anything else other than these are combat or offensive activities, assault activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D00-2798 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not a question has been asked effectively other than to read out a document that we can all see. It's clear -- he wasn't even asked whether he had ever seen this before. I have no objection to the Defence putting in the documents in a proper way, but this is not the proper way. This witness is not being asked for anything other than read what we can all see on the screen. He can't comment on the document because he hasn't seen them before, and they were issued by the government of Bosnia. As I say, no objection to the documents going in, but in a proper fashion. And this witness is not the person to put the documents in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I, for one, do not quite understand the implications of the paragraph that we see on the screen. Unfortunately I do not have the entire document in front of me, so I can only see what we can see on the screen, and that seems to suggest that the planning and launching of combat activities throughout the territory of the republic of BiH is to be accelerated. And I understand that this was done in response to the decision made by the Muslim and Croat parts to secede from the old state of Bosnia, if I can put it that way, but maybe I misunderstand. So if you could clarify with the witness, Mr. Cvijetic, the planning and launching of combat activities throughout the territory of BiH, which event triggered this decision and order to plan and launch combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, my objection is still that how can the witness really answer that one either? He is looking at a document that, although he wasn't asked, I anticipate him to say he has never seen before. He wasn't then part of the government. This is well after -- this is after April the 6th, when the two sides had split. He was part of the Serbian government. This is the BiH government. This document has got nothing to do with this witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, there you go. That's one misunderstanding that I was led into.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the -- that's the problem with this. That is why I'm objecting, saying that this is not the witness to deal with these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I, with the witness and with you, the document I'm showing you to the witness in the context of the witness's assertion that one event, according to him, was the main cause of what he was talking about, that his government must work in wartime, non-peacetime conditions, and that that was an attack on the column of the Yugoslav People's Army. I would like to show only how this attack occurred and who stands behind it, and if that is not in the context of what the witness said, then I don't even know how to be talking about this topic at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection. I think there is a real misunderstanding by Mr. Cvijetic of how to deal with cross-examination. He can certainly put to the witness that the attack on the JNA army, people's army, whatever it was, took place on whatever date and that was it was an attack by the Bosniaks. But what he can't do is show him a series of documents about which this witness doesn't know anything and is simply not even being asked a question about the documents; he is being asked to read out paragraphs of it. As I say, the documents can come in through a witness who is a properly qualified to deal with it or through the Defence case or through a bar table motion, but not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, we agree, so we accept the objection made by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I didn't mean to tender the document into evidence. And from what I understand of your decision, I take it that you do not permit the witness to say anything about this document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There isn't much he can say apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would remind you of his first answer that he said he -- to you, he said he had never seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he also said that paragraph 4 of the order is very clear to him and that he now knows what this is about. In any case, we can ask Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's clear to me too, Mr. Cvijetic. You could ask me. You could ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, from what you've seen, were you able to conclude how this attack occurred and who stands behind it? There, we don't have to put it any other way.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean, how did it come about?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but this is really -- it's time wasting as well. He can read the document, and he can make an educated guess. As His Honour Judge Delvoie has pointed out, Mr. Cvijetic, so can we all. That's not the purpose of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, when you said that one of the events that generated the problems that you spoke about was the attack on the JNA columns, did you think of the attack in Sarajevo, Tuzla, on the attacks on barracks, individual attacks that followed; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, well, I hope that I was clear, and I'm going to repeat that again. The government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time had the best intentions together with the governments of the other ethnic groups to build Bosnia and Herzegovina. We had the best intentions, peacetime intentions. And I'm convinced, I repeat, that we would have been successful in that had two unfortunate events not taken place, the definite rejection of the Cutileiro plan and the attack on the Yugoslav People's Army as it was withdrawing. We are talking about Sarajevo, Tuzla, and the barracks before that, but primarily about the attack on the army columns at that time, and this created an inflammable situation that could get out of control. And this document, please, I said I didn't see it. I said that I didn't see it. But now I see that having this in view anyway, you could not expect the army to withdraw peacefully. You could not expect that on the basis of this document, whereas we believe that all of that would proceed nicely. Now when I see this document it's all clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the point of my showing the document, but since the Trial Chamber decided that I cannot show it to you, at least you did answer the question, so thank you for that anyway, and I need to continue. Mr. Djeric, other than these political problems at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, much of that had an effect on you as well having to start your mandate with major and serious problems that needed to be resolved. You would agree with me that now even within Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of its system, that it had -- what happened was the multilayered collapse of the same; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So other than the things that we talked about in terms of the economy, tourism, transport system, the telecommunications system, what occurred was total disruption and breaking apart?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything just collapsed, all the mechanisms were weakening, the state was weakening, dissolving, effective power was disappearing and problems were piling up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. And what also occurred was the territorial division, are you aware, Mr. Djeric, that as early as 1991, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was formed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about it, but I don't know any particulars or the dates and things like that. But I know that this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And there was a division, unfortunately, along the line of the front between the part that was controlled by the Serbs and the part that was controlled by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, these facts, these particulars, I really don't -- I mean, remember these details, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about details.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what -- I mean, there was a conflict and there was a separation, that did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So this precipitated the crisis even more, did it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: However, Republika Srpska was facing its own problems, was it not? One part of the territory, the western part, was physically completely inaccessible for several months to the organs of central power; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which part of the area that is?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the Krajina which was cut off for a long time up until the moment when the corridor was opened, the Posavina corridor, as an elementary condition of life in that area, it's a large area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a large area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Will you explain to the Trial Chamber. Where is that? Where is that region that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krajina is in northwestern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the biggest town is Banja Luka. This is a region which now has about 800.000 inhabitants. And at that time it was physically cut off, could not be supplied, there was no communication. There were no conditions for any kind of life there and in such a situation. The situation was desperate and that caused fervent fear among people for their life and future. A solution was sought to deal with that situation, to find an exit out of such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was the southern part of Republika Srpska in a similar position, maybe not in the same position, ans I'm referring to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The southeastern part of Republika Srpska or, rather, Bosnia and Herzegovina now, with the biggest town being Trebinje, was also in dire straits. Somewhat less complicated and difficult, however, but it was also cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you said cut off, let me just ask you this, how far was that from Pale as the crow flies, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Well, ball park figure, I can't be sure, but let's say it was perhaps 100 kilometres as the crow flies. Conditionally speaking, because I had never measured the distance. But you could simply not get there because of the configuration of the ground. There was no control over the area. The only way you could reach it was via Montenegro, but it was completely cut off from the rest of the territory. So there was no communication with the leadership -- there was no communication with Sarajevo at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You answered my next question to a large extent, so there was no communication with the leadership of Republika Srpska and the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since the territory had been disintegrated, it was difficult to communicate, there was no traffic and transport lines, telephone lines were down. There was no electricity. And to put it simply, the communication was either difficult or non-existent with the leadership. That was part and parcel of the picture. For months the leadership didn't know what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And if you wanted to reach that area physically, you had to enter a neighbouring state and then take it from there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. You had to go to Montenegro, and then from Montenegro you could enter that part of Herzegovina. There was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, was it safe to take the route through the corridor, even after it had been militarily broken through?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't safe. I assure you it wasn't safe. There was no single road that was safe, and corridor was no exception to that. For a long time, those are all narrow passages which served primarily for supplies. It was -- they were life-lines. Oxygen lines, if you will. So it wasn't safe. It wasn't safe in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. I believe that we have managed to portray the physical part of the ambiance and situation as it was in the Republika Srpska when you assumed your duties as prime minister; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, partly because I assumed those duties at the end of March. The situation was on the verge of bursting at the time politically, but we hoped that we would be able to control the situation. However, the events that I've spoken about generated everything else that happened thereafter, and all that put us in an impossible situation after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much time I have to embark on my next topic after this; however, let me say that Republika Srpska also had its internal political problems which awaited you when you became prime minister. Let me tell you what I'm referring to. You inherited a state, as it were, with the concept of regionalisation. At the moment when you became prime minister, that state had so-called Serbian autonomous provinces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you, please, remember how many there were? I'm not insisting on your answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Majevica, Semberija, Birac, Romanija, also known as Sar-Romanija [phoen], Herzegovina, Krajina, and so on and so forth. There were many. There were a lot. It was one of the biggest problems that we faced at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Finish your answer. You started you may as well finish.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started off facing major problems. Firstly there were political problems that we have just tackled.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you, please focus on my question. I'm talking about Serbian autonomous provinces. I am going to be taking you through the rest of my case, but let's talk about provinces first?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had regional unities that were known as Serbian autonomous provinces where local factors ruled, and it was very difficult to communicate with those people, with those authorities. They all had different views of the problems. They all looked after number one. They all dealt with their own local issues, and nobody actually looked at the central government. Everybody saw what had happened with the central governments first in Yugoslavia and then in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so they all started looking after themselves first and foremost. For a long time, I apologise, let me finish. I don't want to take up much time. But let me say that for a long time those provinces would remain to be a factor in the political life of Republika Srpska, firstly in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later on Republika Srpska. That will go on for a long time because they were not prepared to be integrated into the central government for various reasons. It suited the local power wielders or council, or call them what you will, county prefect -- in any case, local power wielders, it suited them to rule the way they wanted, unobstructed from anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since you've already mentioned counts or earls, I believe that in your previous testimony, you called them local feudals or even furors; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having used the term furors, but I did call them feudal lords.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's try and deal with that through my next questions. When we are talking about the Serbian autonomous provinces, did they have an assembly? Did they have a government? Did they even have ministries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how they envisaged things, and that's what they had. That's what they called those things, but as it to what the actual nature of those things was, I don't know. They referred to them as ministries, ministers, and assembly, their regional governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was that a restricting factor when it came to the functioning of the central government and the central bodies of Republika Srpska, especially the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it was not a minor problem, it was a hugely restricting factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you please try and remember when were the Serbian autonomous provinces abolished, and how did that transpire?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I can't give you any dates. I can't even be specific about events. However, up to the moment I resigned, there was a strong influence of those part, and it was only then that things started breaking up little by little. It took months for that reality to be overcome and for the self-governing Serbian autonomous provinces to be forced, to be integrated into the central authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which would then be transformed into Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the months of August or September, perhaps that problem still persisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me jog your memory. I am not asking for you to be well versed in constitutional laws, but what happened to the constitution of Republika Srpska when the Serbian autonomous provinces were abolished around the time when you had already planned or filed your resignation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, when to comes to the facts, it's very difficult for me to remember everything as I sit here today after such a long time. I don't know when things happened. I'm just saying bearing in mind the year, which was the year 1992, when approximately the influence of the autonomous provinces started subsiding as the local factor in place. It remained present all the time, especially in the first part of that year, in the first half of that year, it was a major problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that this problem persisted all the way up to the month of October of that year?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was already on a downward curve, but up to the month of September, it could be felt as a problem. Even up to the month of October. I really can't draw a very clear-cut line. It's very difficult. But I'm sure that it was up to the autumn of 1992 that they were relevant and strong factor, a fact that you had to reckon with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the moment when new measures, the government measures should have taken off across the entire territory, you actually resigned, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that you put it that way, you may be able to establish all sorts of links, but those were things that were happening on parallel. It's not proper to establish a direct link. All that time the government did its best to break up the resistance of the local factor to introduce the rule of law and order. That's why I was talking about a state with the rule of law. And local government certainly contributed to the factor of the autonomous provinces to be minimised. Without the influence of the government, that factor should have never been abolished because there were all sorts of interests at play there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I have the time to do a calculation with you. For how long did the government of Republika Srpska effectively exist and function? And if this is the time for us to break for the day, maybe I shouldn't even start dealing with that issue. I am in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How long do you think you'll be? You have three minutes. Well, there is an administrative matter with which we have to deal, so perhaps this would be a convenient point. Mr. Djeric, your testimony, as you would appreciate, is not complete, and I repeat the warning that I would have given yesterday, and the -- about not communicating with counsel from either side or speaking with anybody outside of the -- outside of the Chamber about your testimony. We trust that you have a safe weekend. And we resume in this Chamber at 2.15 on Monday afternoon. You are now excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will certainly bear in mind the oath and my solemn promise to you, so you shouldn't worry about that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I am sorry, I just realised that I closed the document, but it seems to me that from next week we got a list from OTP with the witnesses to be heard next week, and then we got a mail from Mr. Zecevic from the Defence of Mr. Stanisic giving time for the cross-examination, but it seems to me that we are not talking about the same witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure that I follow you. As far as I see the mail from our colleagues, it contains already the estimation of our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, but on what witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What are the numbers of the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, ST-15, ST-14, ST --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then I got another mail, sorry. With 150, 1-5-0, and 1 -- well, 44, something like that. I got another mail, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, because we were exchanging some mails, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The witnesses for next week as notified by Mr. Smith, are continuation of Mr. Djeric obviously for Monday, ST-15, ST-14, ST-156, ST-28 and ST-144.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we provided our estimation for the whole -- the for the whole list of witnesses until the end of the year to the Prosecution, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so, but certainly for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If we didn't, we have it, and we will provide it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was a communication between myself and Ms. Korner about one specific witness because he had to be rescheduled. Maybe that is the mail that you received, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's okay. I have an old e-mail in front of me. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Returning to the issue of the -- yesterday where we had gone into private session which we would now wish to have recorded as being open session, it's page 2288, lines 4 up to and including page 2290, line 20. Thank you for that. So it only remains form to be to wish everyone a safe and restful weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd of November 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
